title: Dual-core chip-multiprocessor (two cores on one die)
decision: Implement two full processor cores on a single die sharing a centralized on-chip L2 cache, presenting as a symmetric multiprocessor (SMP).
alternatives_or_rejected: Single-core scaling to a wider/larger core; separate L2 caches per core.
rationale: To deliver SMP capability on a single chip, improve aggregate throughput, and simplify multi-chip SMP system design while managing wire delay and complexity at 0.18-micron technology.
outcome: POWER4 shipped as a dual-core processor; two cores shared the on-chip L2 and competed for L3 and memory bandwidth through a shared memory controller.
weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly frames separate-L2 as a rejected alternative versus simply describing the chosen shared-L2 design.

title: Off-chip L3 cache as a backing store rather than larger on-chip L2
decision: Use a moderate-sized on-chip shared L2 cache backed by a large off-chip L3 cache rather than integrating a very large L2 on-chip.
alternatives_or_rejected: Integrating a much larger L2 on-chip; relying solely on off-chip memory without L3.
rationale: On-chip area and wire-delay constraints limited practical L2 size; an off-chip L3 provided high-bandwidth, high-capacity backing store without consuming die area needed for dual cores and logic.
outcome: POWER4 system included an on-chip L2 and an off-chip L3 controlled by on-chip L3 controllers, improving effective memory latency.
weakest_point: The paper may present this as a natural hierarchy rather than an explicit weighed decision with named alternatives.

title: System interconnect: shared-bus fabric for multi-chip SMP
decision: Use a high-frequency shared-bus interconnect (the processor bus) to link multiple POWER4 chips and the memory controller rather than a switch-based interconnect.
alternatives_or_rejected: Crossbar or packet-switched interconnect between chips.
rationale: A shared bus with snooping provided a proven, lower-complexity coherence mechanism for the target 1–4 socket systems; switch complexity was not justified for the targeted system scale.
outcome: Multi-chip POWER4 systems used the shared processor bus with snooping; the design met bandwidth goals for commercial workloads.
weakest_point: The paper may describe the bus without explicitly weighing it against a crossbar alternative; this may be general knowledge dressed as paper content.

title: RAS: checkstop and recovery philosophy
decision: Implement extensive error detection with checkstop on unrecoverable errors and selective recovery/retry for correctable errors, including ECC on caches and buffers.
alternatives_or_rejected: Lockstep redundant cores or full fault-tolerance (rejected as too costly for commercial microprocessor).
rationale: Mainframe-class RAS was a design objective for enterprise systems, but full redundancy was area- and power-prohibitive; detection-plus-checkstop provided a practical middle ground.
outcome: POWER4 included pervasive ECC, parity, and checkstop logic; the paper reports this met enterprise RAS expectations.
weakest_point: Whether lockstep redundancy is explicitly named as a rejected alternative in the paper or is general background knowledge.
